seo.title: AI Negative Prompt Guide: What NOT to Generate (2026)
seo.description: Master negative prompts in AI image generation. Learn how to exclude blurry visuals, extra fingers, watermarks, and unwanted styles in SDXL, Midjourney & text AI.
keywords: what to avoid in AI image prompts

blocks.text: Most people focus entirely on what they want the AI to create. They craft elaborate descriptions of subjects, styles, and settings, then hit generate and hope for the best. When the result comes back with extra fingers, watermark artifacts, or a cluttered background, they sigh and try again.
Here's the secret that separates beginners from professionals: telling an AI what NOT to do is just as powerful as telling it what to do.

Negative promptingâ€”the practice of explicitly instructing an AI to avoid certain elementsâ€”is one of the most underutilized tools in AI image generation. When used correctly, it eliminates entire classes of mistakes more efficiently than any amount of positive guidance.
This guide will teach you everything you need to know about negative prompts: what they are, how they work, exactly what to write, and the common pitfalls that can ruin your results.
What Is a Negative Prompt?

A negative prompt is exactly what it sounds like: instructions that tell the AI what to exclude from the generation process. Think of it as a filter that reduces the probability of unwanted elements appearing in your final output.

In practical terms, when you generate an image with a positive prompt like "a professional business portrait," the AI might produce results with blurry backgrounds, distorted faces, extra fingers, or random watermarks. Adding a negative prompt such as "blurry, distorted face, extra fingers, watermark, low quality" tells the model to actively avoid these problems.
It works because the model evaluates both your positive and negative instructions simultaneously. It prioritizes the elements you want while actively suppressing the elements you've excluded.

Negative prompts aren't just for images. They're increasingly used for AI writing, video generation, audio platforms, design software, and coding assistance. In writing, you might specify: "Avoid jargon, passive voice, repetitive phrases, and promotional language" to create cleaner, more readable content.
Why Negative Prompts Work

Negative prompts work because they set guardrails rather than just preferences. When you tell the model to avoid something, you're establishing what experts call a "feasibility boundary" rather than just a preference gradient.

This distinction is important. Positive guidance like "be concise" only narrows the output distribution without hard-cutting anything. The model can still produce verbose responses that it subjectively considers "concise enough." Negative constraints like "avoid sentences over 20 words" are binary and verifiable. The model either produced a long sentence or it didn't.

In image generation, this means if you're tired of seeing deformed hands, adding "deformed hands, extra fingers, fused fingers" to your negative prompt gives the model a clear boundary to avoidâ€”something that more vaguely saying "perfect hands" doesn't achieve.

blocks.title: The Mechanics of Negative Guidance
blocks.text: During generation, negative constraints remove entire token sequences from consideration. They create a binary, discrete effect rather than a soft preference. In testing, users who implemented targeted negative prompts reduced post-generation edits from roughly 8 steps down to 3 on portrait batches.
Essential Negative Prompt Categories
To build effective negative prompts, it helps to understand the categories of problems you're trying to avoid.
Quality Issues
These catch common technical flaws that plague AI generations regardless of subject matter.

rows: blurry, soft focus, out of focus, lowres
watermark, signature, username, text, caption, logo
cropped, cut off, out of frame, off-center
oversaturated, washed out, monotone, flat lighting

blocks.title: Baseline Quality Default
blocks.text: Use these as your baseline quality defaults. Start with a small set like "blurry, low quality, pixelated, distorted" for almost every generation.
Anatomy and Structure Issues
This category is crucial for human subjects but applies broadly to any generation where structural coherence matters.

rows: extra fingers, fused fingers, missing fingers, deformed hands, too many fingers
extra limbs, extra arms, extra legs, floating limbs, disconnected limbs
misaligned eyes, cross-eyed, distorted face, duplicate face, asymmetrical eyes
bad anatomy, bad proportions, malformed, disfigured, mutated
duplicated objects, cloned face, mirrored, collage

blocks.title: Targeted Selection Rule
blocks.text: Don't stack all of these at once. Add the specific terms that match the failures you're actually seeing, then test again.
Style and Medium Issues
When you want a photorealistic image, you might want to exclude styles that don't fit.

rows: cartoon, anime, sketch, illustration, painting, 3D render
digital art, vector, watercolor, oil painting

blocks.text: Unwanted Content

rows: modern, futuristic, vintage (when aiming for specific era)

blocks.text: How to Write Effective Negative Prompts
Writing negative prompts isn't difficult, but it requires a different mindset than writing positive prompts. Here are the principles that work:
1. Start With Common Issues
Before you can tell the AI what to avoid, you need to know what problems your generations typically produce. Common starting points include:

items: Blurry visuals
Extra objects or limbs
Poor anatomy
Unrealistic colors
Watermarks
Text artifacts

blocks.text: 2. Use Clear, Specific Terms
Specific language works better than vague descriptors:

rows: asymmetrical eyes, extra fingers, bad proportions
duplicate objects, floating limbs, unnatural colors

blocks.text: 3. Keep It Concise

More isn't always better. Using too many negative prompts can confuse the model and reduce creativity. Aim for 8-12 terms maximum. If you're listing 20+ things to avoid, your main prompt might need work instead.
4. Match Negative Strength to Problem Severity
For persistent issues, repetition increases the negative weight without needing numerical controls. If extra fingers are a chronic problem, try: "extra fingers, too many fingers, deformed fingers".
5. Use Positive + Negative Together
This is where the real power emerges. Combine a clear positive directive with targeted negative constraints:

blocks.title: Positive Directive
blocks.prompt: A professional business portrait in a modern office, natural lighting, sharp focus.

blocks.title: Targeted Negative Constraint
blocks.prompt: blurry, low quality, watermark, extra fingers, distorted face, cartoon style

blocks.text: The 3:1 Rule: Positive vs. Negative Balance

An important principle from prompt engineering is that models generally do better with a short positive guide plus a small set of refusals. A commonly recommended ratio is roughly 3:1 positive to negative instructions.
Positive Prompt Length : Negative Prompt Length = 3 : 1
This means if your positive prompt is 75 words, your negative prompt should be around 25 words. Don't let the negative prompt outweigh the positive one.

blocks.title: Why Ratio Matters
blocks.text: Long lists of 'don't do X' can confuse the model. The AI is fundamentally designed to generate what you ask forâ€”it's better at understanding what things are than what they aren't. Give it direction first, then constraints.
Platform-Specific Negative Prompting
Different AI tools handle negative prompts differently:

items.title: Stable Diffusion (SDXL)
items.description: Words surrounded with [brackets] are read as negative prompts, telling the model to exclude those descriptors from the generation process.

items.title: Picsart
items.description: Find the 'Advanced settings' or 'Negative prompt' field in the AI Image Generator settings.

items.title: Z-Image
items.description: Negative prompts apply a separate conditioning stream that pushes away from listed tokens during sampling. Bump guidance (+0.5) if the refiner reintroduces unwanted elements.

items.title: General Text AI (ChatGPT, Claude, etc.)
items.description: State what to avoid directly in instructions, e.g.: 'Rewrite this professionally. Avoid casual tone, jokes, and emojis.'

blocks.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid
1. Using Too Many Negative Prompts

Adding dozens of restrictions can confuse the model and reduce creativity. Aim for 8-12 terms maximum. In testing, overstuffing the negative prompt beyond roughly 200 characters led to muted contrast and under-detail.
2. Using Vague Negative Language
Terms like "bad image" or "ugly" provide little guidance to the model. Be specific about what you're trying to avoid.
3. Using Conflicting Instructions

blocks.right: Be concise in 3-4 sentences. Avoid examples and long introductions.

blocks.text: 4. Using "Never" Loosely
AI interprets "never" loosely. Use "avoid," "do not," or "exclude" instead of absolute terms the model may not respect.
5. Neglecting Iteration
Prompt engineering is rarely a one-shot process. Review your output, identify remaining flaws, add specific negatives, and regenerate. The best results come from iteration.
Ready-to-Use Negative Prompt Templates

blocks.title: Portrait Photography Template

blocks.title: Product Photography Template

blocks.title: Illustration Style Template

blocks.title: The "Minimum Viable" Template (For Beginners)
blocks.prompt: blurry, low quality, pixelated, distorted, watermark, text

blocks.text: Beyond Image Generation
Negative prompting extends well beyond visual content. Here are some powerful applications across writing, coding, and tone control:

items.title: Writing & Content Generation
items.description: "Write a beginner-friendly article on cloud computing. Avoid jargon, avoid technical complexity, avoid promotional language."

items.title: Coding Assistance
items.description: "Generate Python code for data cleaning. Avoid deprecated libraries, avoid unnecessary comments, avoid inefficient loops."

items.title: Professional Tone Control
items.description: "Rewrite this professionally. Avoid casual tone, jokes, and emojis."

items.title: Hallucination Prevention
items.description: "Summarize this document. Do not add any information not present in the text."

items.title: Creative Control
items.description: "Write a short bio. Avoid storytelling. Avoid exaggeration. Just the facts."

blocks.text: The Secret Trick: Let Positive + Negative Work Together
This is where power really multiplies. The combined approach shapes tone, structure, length, and constraints simultaneously:

blocks.title: Combined Guidance Example
blocks.prompt: Write a 4-sentence explanation of Kubernetes. Be simple and friendly. Avoid jargon. Avoid technical complexity. Avoid examples unless explicitly asked.

blocks.text: Quick Reference Summary
Negative prompts tell AI what to exclude. Use them to:

items: Eliminate blurry, low-quality outputs
Prevent anatomical errors (extra fingers, distorted faces)
Remove unwanted watermarks, text, and logos
Exclude specific styles or objects
Reduce hallucinations and irrelevant details

blocks.text: Write effective negatives by:

items: Using specific terms, not vague descriptors
Keeping your list to 8-12 terms maximum
Starting with common issues, then iterating
Pairing negatives with clear positive instructions
Following roughly 3:1 positive-to-negative ratio
Testing, reviewing, and refining

blocks.text: Remember: Negative prompts are guardrails, not manifestos. Keep them targeted, test them, prune what doesn't work, and watch your AI generations transform from generic to professional.

seo.description: Master AI image prompts with our complete beginner cheat sheet. Learn the core prompt formula, lighting, composition, camera settings, and model-specific tips.

blocks.text: The Problem

You've seen the images. Jaw-dropping visuals that look like they belong in a gallery or a high-budget ad campaign. You type a prompt into the same AI tool. What you get back is... disappointing. Flat. Generic. Obviously AI.
The difference isn't luck or a secret paid tier. It's the prompt.

Most beginners make the same mistake: they treat the AI like a search engine, typing in a few keywords and hoping for the best. But AI image models aren't search engines. They're visual interpreters that need clear, structured instructions to deliver the image in your head. This cheat sheet gives you exactly what you need to go from vague prompts to professional results. No fluff. No jargon. Just actionable techniques you can use right now.
The One Rule to Remember
Every effective prompt has the same basic structure. Think of it as a formula:
Subject + Setting + Style + Lighting + Composition + Mood
You don't need all of these every time. But the more dimensions you specify, the more control you have over the output.
What This Means for You

A blank prompt box is intimidating. Using this structure gives you a starting point. You're not guessing anymoreâ€”you're following a proven framework that works across Midjourney, DALL-E, Gemini, Stable Diffusion, and most other major tools.
The Core Prompt Structure at a Glance
1. The Subject: Don't Just Say "A Woman"
How you describe the main subject shapes everything downstream.

rows: "a woman in her early 40s, relaxed expression, natural makeup, wearing a linen shirt, looking slightly off-camera"
"a confident man in his 50s, in a well-lit office, slight smile, not looking at the camera"
"a golden retriever puppy with floppy ears, lying on grass, tongue slightly out"

blocks.title: What to Specify for Subjects
blocks.text: Approximate age, expression, posture, clothing style, eye contact direction, and mood.
2. The Setting: Be Specific About the Environment

rows: "a narrow cobblestone street in an old European city at dusk, ambient yellow streetlights, few pedestrians"
"ancient redwood forest floor, morning mist, shafts of light filtering through the canopy"
"a cozy living room with a fireplace, warm wooden furniture, and a large window showing a snowy landscape"

blocks.text: 3. Style: Tell the AI How It Should Look
Style keywords tell the AI which part of its training data to draw from. This is one of the fastest ways to get coherent, distinctive results.

blocks.text: 4. Lighting: The Secret to Professional Results
Lighting is the single variable with the biggest impact on whether an image looks professional or amateur. Here's a quick reference:

rows: Subject outlined by light against dark background

blocks.title: The Catchlight Trick
blocks.text: For portraits, make sure to add "catchlight in eyes" or "light reflecting in eyes." Without this, eyes can look flat or "dead." It's a tiny addition that makes a massive difference.
5. Composition: Frame the Shot Like a Photographer

rows: Fills the frame with subject detail
Shows the subject in full environmental context
Looking up at the subject, dramatic perspective
Subject offset to one side, compositionally balanced
Implies the perspective of another person in the scene
Significant empty area around the subjectâ€”good for text overlay
Architectural or natural elements that draw the eye toward the subject

blocks.text: 6. Mood: Translate Feelings into Visual Terms

rows: Soft morning light, gentle mist, muted colors
Fog, shadows, low-key lighting, hidden faces, deep blue tones
Overcast sky, desaturated colors, empty spaces, rain, long shadows
Bright sunlight, vibrant colors, open spaces, warm golden tones
Dramatic lighting, shallow depth of field, film grain, wide aspect ratio

blocks.text: 7. Quality Modifiers
Words like "highly detailed," "photorealistic," "4K resolution," "sharp focus," "hyperrealistic" can encourage the AI to produce more refined images.

blocks.title: Example Quality-Enhanced Prompt
blocks.prompt: A dramatic portrait of a woman with striking features, illuminated by warm golden hour light, highly detailed, sharp focus, photorealistic.

blocks.text: Build Smarter: Use the Prompt Formula
The Universal One-Liner Template
Subject, medium, style, lighting, framing, mood, palette.

blocks.title: Universal One-Liner Example
blocks.prompt: Portrait of a barista, film photo, soft rim light, 50mm close-up, warm mood, teal-orange palette.

blocks.text: The Full-Structure Template

A photorealistic [shot type] of [subject], [action or expression], set in [environment]. The scene is illuminated by [lighting description], creating a [mood] atmosphere. Captured with a [camera/lens details], emphasizing [key textures and details].

blocks.title: Full-Structure Template Example
blocks.prompt: A photorealistic close-up portrait of an elderly Japanese ceramicist with deep, sun-etched wrinkles and a warm, knowing smile. He is carefully inspecting a freshly glazed tea bowl. The setting is his rustic, sun-drenched workshop. The scene is illuminated by soft, golden hour light streaming through a window, highlighting the fine texture of the clay. Captured with an 85mm portrait lens, resulting in a soft, blurred background (bokeh). The overall mood is serene and masterful.

blocks.text: The Structure-First Approach (For DiT Models)
If you're using modern transformer-based models (like Gemini or Flux), the order of your prompt matters. These models generate from whole to part, so framework belongs at the start:
Composition â†’ Lighting â†’ Depth of Field â†’ Angle â†’ Subject â†’ Environment â†’ Details

blocks.title: Structure-First Prompt Example
blocks.prompt: Asymmetrical composition, subject on left third, soft side lighting, shallow depth of field with focus on eyes, low angle view, a woman with long black hair and red dress, standing in a rainy city street, glowing neon reflections on wet pavement.

blocks.text: Platform-Specific Cheat Sheet
Different AI models have different strengths. Here's what works best for each:

items.title: Gemini (Nano Banana)
items.description: Use full, narrative sentences. A descriptive paragraph will almost always produce better results than a list of keywords. Specify "high resolution" for best output.

items.title: Midjourney
items.description: Use natural language with commas separating concepts. Add parameters at the end such as --ar 16:9, --stylize 250, --chaos 20.

items.title: DALL-E
items.description: Handles detailed, full-sentence descriptions well. Natural language works bestâ€”no special parameters needed.

items.title: Stable Diffusion
items.description: More technical prompts often work better. Use weighted tokens: (term:1.2) for more emphasis, [term] for less. Negative prompts are particularly important.

items.title: Flux
items.description: Prompts can be shorter than for other modelsâ€”the model does heavy lifting. Use Flux Pro for final assets, Flux Dev for rapid iteration.

blocks.text: Negative Prompts: What to Avoid
Some tools have a dedicated negative prompt field. Others respond to plain-language instructions like "avoid" or "do not include".

blocks.title: Positive Prompting Rule
blocks.text: AI models are better at understanding what things are than what they aren't. Instead of saying "no blurry," describe what you want: "crisp focus, sharp details".
Common Negative Prompts

items: No text
No logos
No watermarks
No extra objects
No distorted hands
No extra fingers
No cropped subject
No unrealistic colors
No busy background
No duplicate products
No blurry details

blocks.text: Alternative Approach
If the AI keeps adding an element you don't want, use positive prompting instead. Tell the AI what you do want, not what you don't.
Common Mistakes to Avoid
1. Being Too Vague

blocks.right: A black electric sports car parked on a wet city street at night, neon reflections, low camera angle, cinematic lighting, realistic photography.

blocks.text: 2. Adding Too Many Conflicting Details

blocks.left: A minimalist futuristic vintage rustic cyberpunk watercolor photorealistic poster of a coffee shop in a spaceship forest.
blocks.right: A cozy futuristic coffee shop inside a glass space station, warm lighting, realistic cinematic style, view of stars through large windows.

blocks.text: 3. Forgetting the Output Format
If the image is for a real channel, include the format:

items: Wide hero image
Square social post
Vertical story image
Product card thumbnail
Email banner
Blog header

blocks.text: 4. Asking for Too Much Text
AI image models can struggle with long copy. Keep text short (under 25 characters) or add it later in post-production.
How to Iterate: From Okay to Great
Step 1: Start Broad
Generate a basic version of your idea to see what the AI understands.
Step 2: Analyze the Results
What worked? What didn't? What's missing?
Step 3: Refine One Element at a Time
Add one detail, run again, then add the next. This way you know exactly what improved (or hurt) the output.
Step 4: Use Variations
Generate 4-8 variations of the same prompt. Minor differences in phrasing can yield dramatically different results.
Step 5: Use Your First Results to Write Better Prompts

A great technique is to let the AI write its own prompt. Ask a chatbot to generate a prompt for the image you want, then use that prompt with your image generator. The AI knows exactly what its image generator responds to best.

blocks.title: Chatbot Prompt Generation Example
blocks.prompt: I would like to create an image of a sunset over a mountain range. Generate a detailed prompt that I can use to request this image from [AI generator].

blocks.text: The AI will automatically include lighting, style, and composition details you wouldn't have thought to add.
Quick Reference: Prompt Templates

blocks.title: Template for Any Scene
blocks.prompt: A [photorealistic] [shot type] of [subject], [action or expression], set in [environment]. The scene is illuminated by [lighting description], creating a [mood] atmosphere. Captured with a [camera/lens details], emphasizing [key textures and details]. [Aspect ratio format].

blocks.title: Template for Product Images
blocks.prompt: A realistic product image of [product] on [surface/background], [lighting], [composition], [style], [mood], no text, no extra objects.

blocks.title: Template for Blog Headers
blocks.prompt: A wide blog header image for an article about [topic], showing [main visual], [style], [color palette], [composition], no readable text.

blocks.title: Template for Social Posts
blocks.prompt: A square social media image for [brand/category], featuring [subject], [background], [lighting], [mood], space for a short headline.

blocks.title: Template for Prompt Editing
blocks.prompt: Use the uploaded image. Keep [subject] unchanged. Change [specific element] to [new element]. Match [lighting/style]. Avoid [things to avoid].

blocks.text: Final Checklist
Run through this before hitting "generate":

items: âœ… Is my subject specific and clearly described?
âœ… Have I kept the prompt focused on 2-3 key elements?
âœ… Did I specify style, medium, or artistic technique?
âœ… Have I included composition and framing details?
âœ… Is my aspect ratio specified?
âœ… Am I using positive language instead of negative constraints?
âœ… Have I translated abstract concepts into concrete visual terms?
âœ… Is my prompt length appropriate for the platform I'm using?
âœ… Did I include lighting and atmosphere descriptors?

blocks.text: Conclusion
Writing effective AI image prompts is a skill, not a magic trick. It takes practice, experimentation, and a willingness to learn from both successes and failures.

Start with one technique from this cheat sheet on your next prompt. Add a lighting descriptor. Try a structure-first prompt. Use the "let the AI write its own prompt" trick. Each improvement brings you closer to images that look like they came from a professional.
The models can do it. They just need you to tell them exactly what to do.
Happy prompting!

blocks.text: Cinematic AI image prompts are among the most searched and most copied prompts in any AI image library. They capture something that simpler prompts miss: the feeling that an image was taken from a movie frame, lit by a professional gaffer, and composed by a director with a clear visual language. This guide gives you 50 ready-to-use cinematic prompts and explains the mechanics behind each one so you can adapt them to your own projects.
What Makes a Prompt Cinematic?

A cinematic image is not simply a photograph with a film grain filter added in post. It combines several technical and aesthetic decisions that work together. The first is aspect ratio. Cinema uses wide formats such as 2.39:1 anamorphic, 2.35:1, or 16:9 widescreen, that put the subject inside a wider horizontal space and give the frame a sense of scale that portrait formats cannot achieve.

The second is depth of field. Cinematic images often use large apertures that separate the subject from the background with a distinct blur, known as bokeh. This isolation focuses the viewer's attention and creates a professional, intentional look that distinguishes movie imagery from documentary snapshots.

The third is colour grading. Film and digital cinema apply colour treatments that go beyond simple brightness and contrast adjustments. Teal-and-orange is the most recognizable: shadows shift toward cool blue-green tones while skin tones are pushed toward warm amber. Other common grades include bleach bypass which is desaturated and high-contrast, cross-processed colours, and the warm golden tones of 1970s analogue film.

The fourth is intentional lighting. Cinematic images are lit with purpose. Rim lights separate subjects from dark backgrounds. Practical lights such as lamps, neon signs, and fire appear in frame and create motivation for the light direction. Volumetric fog or haze catches rays of light and creates atmosphere. Together these elements signal that the image was constructed, not discovered.
Portrait Cinematic Prompts (1 to 15)

Portrait prompts work best when they combine a clear subject description with specific lighting and mood directions. The model needs to know who the subject is, what they are doing or feeling, and what the light source is. Generic portrait prompts without these details produce stock-photography results, not cinematic stills.

If the generated image is close but not exactly right, identify the one element that needs fixing, usually lighting or colour grade, and add a more specific instruction to address only that element. Over-correcting by rewriting the whole prompt tends to lose the qualities that were already working.

seo.description: Master realistic AI photo prompts with our comprehensive guide. Learn lens behavior, lighting techniques, camera specs, composition, and 15 ready-to-use prompts.

blocks.text: The difference between a plastic-looking AI image and a photo that could pass for real comes down to one thing: how you prompt.

You've seen the look. Skin like a wax figure. Lighting that comes from everywhere and nowhere. A background so uniformly sharp it feels like a green screen. Every surface slightly too glossy, every color slightly too saturated. That's the AI lookâ€”and if it's the reason you've been hesitant to experiment with AI image generation, you're not alone.
The good news? The gap between "obviously AI" and "wait, that's generated?" is almost entirely a prompting problem. The models can do it. They just need better instructions.
In this complete guide, you'll learn exactly how to write AI photography prompts that produce images so realistic, they'll fool even trained eyes.
Why AI Defaults to "Plastic"
Understanding the problem makes it easier to fix.

AI image generators are trained on massive datasets, and a disproportionate chunk of those images are retouched stock photographyâ€”the kind where skin has been smoothed to oblivion, lighting is studio-flat, and everything sits at the same focal distance.

When you give the model a vague prompt, it reaches for the statistical average of its training data. And the statistical average of heavily retouched photography is, predictably, images that look heavily retouched.
Every detail you leave undefined gets filled with the most "polished" version the model has learned:

items: No lighting specified? You get flat, diffused light from every direction
No skin texture mentioned? You get airbrushed porcelain
No depth of field called out? Everything stays sharp from foreground to background

blocks.text: The result is technically clean but visually lifeless.

blocks.title: Mindset Shift
blocks.text: When you hire a photographer, you trust them to make the technical decisions. An AI model doesn't have that instinct. It has capability without taste. So when you're prompting, you're not the client giving a briefâ€”you're the photographer behind the camera, making every creative call yourself.
The Single Biggest Shift: Write Shot Descriptions, Not Prompts
The single biggest shift you can make is to stop writing AI prompts and start writing shot descriptions.

AI models understand camera language because their training data is tagged with it. When you specify a lens, a focal length, and a shooting style, the model pulls from a completely different part of its visual libraryâ€”one that includes optical behavior, depth separation, and the natural way light falls off across a frame.
Compare these two approaches:

blocks.left: A woman standing in a field of flowers, realistic, high quality, 8K
blocks.right: Candid portrait of a woman standing in a wildflower field, shot on 85mm lens at f/1.8, golden hour side lighting from the right, soft bokeh in background, natural skin texture with visible pores, slight motion in hair, shot on Fujifilm X-T5

blocks.text: The first prompt tells the model almost nothing useful. "Realistic" and "high quality" are the AI equivalent of asking a photographer for "good photos". The second prompt gives the model everything it needs to produce something believable.
The 5 Essential Elements of a Realistic AI Photo Prompt
Professional-quality photo prompts specify five key elements: subject, lighting, composition, lens behavior, and mood.
1. Subject (The "What")
Be specific about who or what is in the frame. Instead of "a person," try:

items: "A middle-aged woman with curly salt-and-pepper hair, laugh lines around her eyes, wearing a worn denim jacket"
"A weathered wooden fishing boat with peeling blue paint, rusted hardware, and coiled rope on the deck"

blocks.title: Key Insight: Build Imperfection
blocks.text: Build imperfection into your prompts deliberately. For portraits, specify "visible skin pores, natural blemishes, slight facial asymmetry"â€”these cues tell the model to pull from its more candid, less retouched training data.
2. Lighting (The "How It's Lit")
Lighting is arguably the most important element for realism. Generic lighting produces flat, lifeless images. Specific lighting creates depth, mood, and believability.

rows: "warm golden hour light from the right, long soft shadows"
"soft natural window light from camera-left, diffused through sheer curtains"
"rim lighting from behind, creating a bright edge around the subject"
"soft overcast daylight, gentle shadows, muted contrast"
"softbox key light from above-left, fill light from right, clean white background"

blocks.text: Instead of generic terms like "good lighting," specify exactly what you want.
3. Lens and Camera Details (The "Technical Specs")
This is the secret weapon of realistic AI prompts. Camera and lens terminology steers realism more reliably than generic terms like "8K" or "ultra-detailed".
Common lenses to reference:

rows: Wide angle, captures more of the scene

blocks.text: Camera brands to reference:

items: "Shot on Canon EOS R5"
"Shot on Fujifilm X-T5"
"Shot on Sony A7III"
"iPhone photo"

blocks.text: Aperture (f-stop) references:

items: f/1.4 - f/2.8: Shallow depth of field, blurred background
f/5.6 - f/8: Moderate depth, good for groups
f/11 - f/16: Deep focus, everything sharp

blocks.text: 4. Composition and Framing (The "How It's Framed")
Specify how the subject fills the frame:

rows: Focus on a single feature (eye, texture, detail)

blocks.text: Camera angles:

items: Eye-level: Neutral, relatable
Low-angle: Powerful, imposing
High-angle: Vulnerable, small
Dutch angle: Uneasy, tense

blocks.text: 5. Mood and Atmosphere (The "Feel")
Translate abstract moods into concrete visual terms:

rows: Soft morning light, gentle mist, muted colors
Overcast sky, desaturated tones, rain, long shadows
High contrast, strong shadows, bold lighting
Warm tones, shallow depth of field, close framing

blocks.text: Advanced Techniques for Photorealism
1. Reference Specific Film Stocks and Eras
Naming specific film stocks or photography eras gives the AI a distinctive look to aim for:

items: "Kodak Portra 400" â€“ Warm, slightly desaturated, classic film look
"Fujifilm Pro 400H" â€“ Cooler, pastel tones
"Ilford HP5" â€“ Classic black and white film, noticeable grain
"80s Kodak film photo, slight grain, warm colors, candid snapshot feel"

blocks.text: 2. Use "Photorealistic" and Its Cousins
Use the word "photorealistic" directly when realism is the goal. Or swap in close cousins like:

items: "real photograph"
"taken on a real camera"
"professional photography"
"iPhone photo"

blocks.text: 3. Add Imperfections Deliberately
Real photos have imperfections. Add them to your prompt:

items: "slight motion blur in background elements"
"subtle lens flare"
"natural grain, slight noise"
"imperfect framing, slightly off-center"
"candid, unposed moment"

blocks.text: 4. Specify Texture and Detail
Be concrete about materials, shapes, and textures:

items: "visible pores, fine wrinkles, natural skin texture"
"weathered wood grain, peeling paint"
"rough concrete surface with minor cracks"
"fabric wear on denim, slight fraying at edges"

blocks.text: 5. Use the "Quality-Latency" Lever

For high-volume or latency-sensitive use cases, start with a lower quality setting and evaluate whether it meets your requirements. Step up to medium or high for close-up portraits, small text, and identity-sensitive edits.
Platform-Specific Prompting Tips
For Gemini (Nano Banana)
Gemini's core strength is its deep language understanding. A narrative, descriptive paragraph will almost always produce a better, more coherent image than a simple list of disconnected words.
Template from Google:

Captured with a [camera/lens details], emphasizing [key textures and details]. The image should be in a [aspect ratio] format.

items: --ar 16:9 for aspect ratio

blocks.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid

items: âŒ Vague Language: Words like "nice" or "beautiful" don't give the AI much to work with. Specify the type of light, the mood, or the setting instead.
âŒ Conflicting Instructions: Mixing cues like "harsh sunlight" and "soft dreamy look" forces the tool to split the difference, often producing awkward results.
âŒ Ignoring Composition: Without guidance on framing or perspective, the subject may appear off-balance or cropped in unhelpful ways.
âŒ Overloading with Detail: Adding too many unrelated descriptors can confuse the output. Stick to the elements that actually shape the photo.
âŒ Forgetting Color and Tone: If you leave the palette undefined, you may end up with clashing hues or lighting that doesn't match.

âŒ Using "No" in Negative Prompts: Instead of saying "no blur," describe what you want: "crisp focus, sharp details." Google explicitly recommends avoiding "semantic negative prompts" that use "no" or "without."

blocks.text: Quick Reference: Realistic AI Photo Prompt Template
Use this template structure for any realistic AI photo:

A [photorealistic] [shot type] of [subject], [action or expression], set in [environment]. The scene is illuminated by [lighting description], creating a [mood] atmosphere. Captured with a [camera/lens details], emphasizing [key textures and details]. [Aspect ratio format].

The scene is illuminated by soft window light from the left, creating a warm intimate atmosphere. Captured with an 85mm lens at f/1.8, emphasizing visible skin texture and natural eye highlights. Vertical portrait orientation.

blocks.text: Conclusion

Creating realistic AI photos isn't about finding the magic phraseâ€”it's about thinking like a photographer. Specify the lighting. Name the lens. Describe the texture. Add the imperfections that make real photos feel alive.
The models are capable of photorealism. They just need you to tell them exactly what to do.

Start with one of the templates above. Add one camera detail. Then add one lighting specification. Each layer of specificity brings you closer to an image that doesn't just look like AIâ€”it looks like a photograph.
Happy shooting!

seo.title: ChatGPT vs Gemini: Which AI is Best for Image Prompts? (2026)
seo.description: Comprehensive comparison between ChatGPT (DALL-E 3) and Google Gemini (Nano Banana) for AI image generation. Prompting styles, quality, consistency, and editing.

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence has transformed image generation, but with so many options available, choosing the right tool can be overwhelming. Two of the most powerful contenders are OpenAI's ChatGPT (powered by DALL-E) and Google's Gemini (with its native Nano Banana image models). Both are impressive, but they excel in different areas.

In this comprehensive guide, we'll compare ChatGPT and Gemini head-to-head across multiple dimensionsâ€”prompting styles, image quality, consistency, editing capabilities, and moreâ€”to help you decide which AI is best for your image creation needs.
The Contenders: A Quick Overview
ChatGPT Images (DALL-E)

ChatGPT's image generation is powered by DALL-E 3, OpenAI's state-of-the-art text-to-image model. When you describe an image in ChatGPT, the model automatically generates tailored, detailed prompts for DALL-E that bring your ideas to life. If you like a particular image but want adjustments, you can ask ChatGPT to make tweaks with just a few words. The system uses GPT-4 to optimize prompts before they're passed to DALL-E, a process called "prompt rewriting".
Gemini Images (Nano Banana)

Gemini's image generation is powered by the Nano Banana family of modelsâ€”native multimodal models built on the Gemini 3 architecture. Unlike systems that bolt image generation onto a language model, Gemini was trained from the ground up to process text and images in a single, unified step. This native multimodal architecture enables powerful capabilities beyond simple image generation, including conversational editing, multi-image composition, and logical reasoning about image content.
Head-to-Head Comparison
1. Prompting Philosophy
The fundamental difference between ChatGPT and Gemini comes down to how they handle prompts.

ChatGPT acts as an intermediary. You describe your idea in plain English, and ChatGPT rewrites it into an optimized prompt for DALL-E. This means you don't need to be a prompt engineering expertâ€”ChatGPT handles the heavy lifting. The model suggests a structure like: subject + environment/background + style + mood/lighting + specific details.

Gemini takes a different approach. With its deep language understanding, Gemini prefers narrative, descriptive paragraphs over keyword lists. The fundamental principle for Gemini prompting is simple: describe the scene, don't just list keywords. A well-written paragraph will almost always produce better results than a disconnected list of words.

Practical Example:
When tested with the same basic requestâ€”"a sunflower made of sheet metal in a pencil drawing style"â€”both tools returned dramatically different prompts:

blocks.left: A pencil drawing of a metal sunflower with sculpted metal pieces, visible welds, detailed shading creating depth, pencil lines visible, set in a garden with blurry plants in the background.
blocks.right: A detailed pencil drawing of a sunflower constructed from sheet metal with visible seams, rivets, and subtle bends; the center composed of layered metal textures; rendered in realistic graphite pencil style with fine linework, cross-hatching, and soft shading; high contrast; minimal background.

blocks.title: Verdict: Prompting Philosophy
blocks.text: Both generated more detail than a typical user would know to add. Gemini suggested a more atmospheric scene (garden with blurry plants), while ChatGPT focused on technical precision (rivets, seams, cross-hatching).
2. Image Quality and Realism

According to a comprehensive 2026 test comparing major AI image generators using identical prompts, Gemini obtained the highest overall score thanks to its consistency, while ChatGPT led in aspects related to visual quality, such as realism and richness of detail.

This aligns with a 2025 test that concluded Gemini "is now more useful than ChatGPT for creating images that look real," with cleaner adherence to scene constraints. ChatGPT, however, excels at producing images with higher visual polish and photorealism.
3. Prompt Adherence and Consistency

Gemini has a notable edge in consistency. It preserves fine-grained detail and adheres reliably to multi-constraint prompts, even with multiple simultaneous requirements. This means if you give Gemini a complex prompt with many specific elements, it's more likely to deliver all of them accurately.

ChatGPT is highly capable but can sometimes reinterpret your request in unexpected ways. The prompt rewriting feature, while helpful, means you're not always seeing exactly what DALL-E receives. If you want to debug, you can ask ChatGPT to display the prompt that was sent to DALL-E.
Gemini's consistency advantage was highlighted in a 2026 ranking where it scored highest overall due to its consistency.
4. Editing Capabilities
This is where the differences become stark.

ChatGPT (DALL-E) allows for conversational editing. You can ask for tweaks with just a few words, and ChatGPT will handle the rest. You can generate variations and use seed numbers to maintain a consistent style. However, editing is primarily done through regenerating with modified prompts.
Gemini (Nano Banana) offers significantly more advanced editing capabilities thanks to its native multimodal architecture:

items: Conversational editing: Add, remove, or modify elements; change style; adjust colors
Multi-image composition: Use multiple input images to compose a new scene or transfer style
Iterative refinement: Progressively refine images over multiple turns
Precise local edits: Make changes to specific parts of an image using simple language
Character consistency: Preserve a character's appearance across multiple generations
Style transfer: Apply a style, texture, or design from one concept to another

blocks.text: Gemini's editing is truly conversational and iterative. You can generate an image, then say "change the lighting to golden hour" or "make the background more dramatic" without starting from scratch.

blocks.title: Verdict: Editing Capabilities
blocks.text: Gemini wins decisively on editing capabilities.
5. Text Rendering
Both models have improved significantly in text rendering, but there are important distinctions.

Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (Nano Banana 2) and Gemini 3 Pro Image (Nano Banana Pro) can generate images that contain clear and well-placed text, making them ideal for logos, diagrams, and posters. However, even Gemini can still struggle with accurate spelling and fine details in images. For best results, provide the exact text you want in quote marks.
ChatGPT also handles text reasonably well but historically has struggled more with text rendering than Gemini's latest models.
6. Technical Specifications
7. Usage Limits
Usage limits can be a deciding factor for heavy users.
ChatGPT typically limits free users and even paid users can hit daily caps. In testing, ChatGPT generated about three to five images before hitting the daily limit.
Gemini and Grok both showed no such limits in testing. However, specific limits may vary by subscription tier.
A Single Prompt Tweak That Makes a Big Difference
Here's a powerful technique that works for both platforms: let the AI write its own prompt.
Instead of struggling to craft the perfect prompt yourself, simply ask the chatbot to generate one for its corresponding image generator:

blocks.title: Meta-Prompting Technique
blocks.prompt: I would like to create an image of [your idea]. Generate a prompt that I can use to request this image from [Nano Banana or ChatGPT Images].

blocks.text: This approach has multiple benefits:

items: The AI knows exactly what its image generator responds to best
It automatically includes details you wouldn't think to add
It avoids language that the generator might flag or refuse

blocks.text: If the generated prompt is too long, simply ask for a shorter version.
Which One Should You Choose?
Choose ChatGPT If:

items: You want the highest visual quality and realism. ChatGPT consistently ranks higher on visual quality and richness of detail.
You prefer a hands-off prompting experience. ChatGPT rewrites your rough ideas into optimized prompts automatically.
You're creating photorealistic or highly polished images.
You don't need extensive iterative editing.

blocks.text: Choose Gemini If:

items: You need consistency across multiple images. Gemini's character consistency and prompt adherence are unmatched.
You want powerful editing capabilities. Conversational editing, multi-image composition, and local edits are Gemini's superpowers.
You need text rendering for logos, posters, or diagrams.
You're building a brand or character that needs to appear consistently across generations.
You want to use reference imagesâ€”Gemini supports up to 14.
You want Google Search grounding for factually accurate images.

blocks.text: The Bottom Line
Both tools are excellent, but they serve different needs:

blocks.title: Summary Verdict
blocks.text: Gemini obtained the highest overall score thanks to its consistency, while ChatGPT led in aspects more related to visual quality, such as realism and richness of detail.

If you need a single, stunning, photorealistic image with minimal effort, ChatGPT is your best bet. If you need to create a series of consistent images, edit them conversationally, or compose complex scenes from multiple references, Gemini is the superior choice.
The Best of Both Worlds
Many professionals use both tools strategically:

items: Use ChatGPT for hero images, marketing visuals, and photorealistic scenes
Use Gemini for brand assets, character consistency, multi-image composition, and iterative editing

blocks.text: The good news? Both platforms are constantly evolving. By 2026, the gap between them has narrowed significantly, and both produce images that would have been unimaginable just a few years ago.
Final Thoughts

The "best" AI for image prompts ultimately depends on your specific needs. ChatGPT excels at producing visually stunning, realistic images with minimal prompting effort. Gemini excels at consistency, editing, and complex multi-image workflows.

Try both. Use the "let the AI write its own prompt" technique for each. See which one delivers results that align with your creative vision. And rememberâ€”the most impressive AI images often come from experimentation and iteration, regardless of which tool you choose.

Understanding the AI Mindset

Think of AI as a brilliant but literal-minded assistant. It doesn't understand context, nuance, or implication in the way humans do. Gemini's Unique Advantage: Native Multimodality

blocks.title: The Golden Rule of Gemini Prompting

The Anatomy of a Great AI Prompt
A well-constructed prompt typically contains several key elements:
1. Subject Matter (The "What")

Clearly state what you want to see in the image. Be specific about the main focus, whether it's a person, object, scene, or abstract concept. Instead of "a dog," try "a golden retriever puppy" or "a cyberpunk-themed robotic wolf."

blocks.title: Gemini Tip: Subject Consistency
blocks.text: Use clear reference images to maintain subject consistency. Assign a distinct name to each character or object in your prompt so the model can follow along and maintain their look as you build out scenes.
2. Style and Medium (The "How")
Specify the artistic style or medium you're aiming for. This is where you can get incredibly creative with options like:

items: Art movements: impressionism, cubism, surrealism, art deco
Mediums: oil painting, watercolor, charcoal sketch, digital art, 3D render
Artist inspirations: "in the style of Salvador Dali" or "reminiscent of Studio Ghibli"
Photography terms: macro photography, long exposure, bokeh effect, cinematic lighting

blocks.title: Gemini Tip: Style Transfer
blocks.text: Gemini excels at style transfer â€“ you can apply a style, texture, or design from one concept to another. For example, "Transform this photograph into the artistic style of Van Gogh's 'Starry Night'."
3. Composition and Framing (The "Where")
Describe how the image should be arranged. Consider elements like:

items: Perspective: bird's eye view, close-up, wide shot, macro
Camera angles: low angle, high angle, Dutch angle
Framing: full body shot, portrait, environmental portrait
Lighting: dramatic lighting, golden hour, studio lighting, moody atmosphere

blocks.text: The official template for photorealistic scenes in Gemini 2.5 Flash includes specific camera and lens details: "A photorealistic [shot type] of [subject], [action or expression], set in [environment]. The scene is illuminated by [lighting description], creating a [mood] atmosphere. Captured with a [camera/lens details], emphasizing [key textures and details]."
4. Color and Mood (The "Feel")
Paint with words to establish the emotional tone and color palette:

items: Mood: serene, chaotic, mysterious, joyful, melancholic
Color schemes: monochromatic, complementary, pastel, vibrant
Atmosphere: foggy, clear, ethereal, gritty, dreamy

1. Think Like a Photographer
For photorealistic images, Google recommends mentioning camera angles, lens types, lighting, and fine details to guide the model toward realistic results.

blocks.text: 2. Leverage Conversational Editing
One of Gemini's standout features is the ability to refine images through conversation. Don't expect perfection on the first try â€“ follow up with prompts like:

items: "That's great, but can you make the lighting a bit warmer?"
"Keep everything the same, but change the character's expression to be more serious."

blocks.text: 3. Use Multi-Image Composition
Gemini can combine up to 14 reference images in a single prompt, maintaining consistency for up to 5 people. This is perfect for creating professional e-commerce fashion photos or creative collages.

blocks.title: Multi-Image Composition
blocks.prompt: Create a professional e-commerce fashion photo. Take the blue floral dress from the first image and let the woman from the second image wear it. Generate a realistic, full-body shot of the woman wearing the dress.

blocks.text: 4. Render Text Accurately
Gemini 3.5 Flash and Gemini 3 Pro can render clear, well-placed text in images â€“ ideal for logos, diagrams, and posters. Enclose your desired words in quotes and describe the typography style:

blocks.title: Text Rendering Prompt
blocks.prompt: Create a modern, minimalist logo for a coffee shop called 'The Daily Grind'. The text should be in a clean, bold, sans-serif font.

blocks.text: 5. Use "Semantic Negative Prompts"
Instead of saying "no cars," describe the desired scene positively: "an empty, deserted street with no signs of traffic". This approach works better across all AI generators.
Practical Prompt Examples

rows: Who or what is in the image? Be specific.

extreme close-up, wide shot, low angle

blocks.text: Advanced Techniques for Gemini
Character Consistency Across Generations

Gemini can maintain the likeness of a person or character across different poses, lighting, and environments. Establish a clearly defined character with specific details in your first prompt, then use follow-up prompts to place that same character in new contexts:

blocks.title: Prompt 1: Establish the Character
blocks.prompt: A whimsical illustration of a tiny, glowing mushroom sprite. The sprite has a large, bioluminescent mushroom cap for a hat, wide, curious eyes, and a body made of woven vines.

blocks.title: Prompt 2: Move to New Context
blocks.prompt: Now, show the same sprite riding on the back of a friendly, moss-covered snail through a sunny meadow.

blocks.text: Precise Local Edits
Make targeted changes to specific parts of an image without re-generating the entire scene:

blocks.title: Local Edit Prompt
blocks.prompt: Using the provided image, change only the blue sofa to be a vintage, brown leather chesterfield sofa. Keep everything else exactly the same.

blocks.text: Use Logic and Reasoning
Gemini's real-world understanding allows it to predict what comes next in a sequence:

blocks.title: Sequence Stage 1
blocks.prompt: Generate an image of a person holding a 3-tiered cake.

blocks.title: Sequence Stage 2 (Physics & Context)
blocks.prompt: Generate an image showing what would happen if they tripped. The model understands the context and physics to simulate a plausible outcome.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid

items: Being Too Vague: 'Create something beautiful' is essentially useless. Be specific about what beauty means in this context.
Overcrowding the Prompt: While detail is good, cramming too many elements can confuse the AI. Focus on the most important aspects and let the AI fill in the rest.
Forgetting About Composition: Many users focus only on subject matter and style, neglecting how the image is framed and composed.
Not Specifying Aspect Ratio: Gemini works best when you specify your desired format, like 4:3, 1:1, or 16:9.

blocks.text: Platform-Specific Considerations
Different AI image generators interpret prompts differently:

items.description: Handles detailed descriptions well. Excels at conceptual combinations. Responds well to style-specific terminology.

blocks.text: Conclusion

Mastering AI image prompts is a journey of continuous learning and experimentation. Start with clear, well-structured descriptions, gradually incorporate more sophisticated techniques, and most importantly, practice regularly. Each generation provides valuable feedback that helps you better understand how to communicate your visual ideas to the AI.

With Gemini's native multimodal architecture, you have powerful tools at your disposal â€“ from conversational editing and multi-image composition to precise local edits and text rendering. Remember the golden rule: describe the scene, don't just list keywords. Provide context and intent, iterate and refine, and don't be afraid to experiment with different prompting strategies.

As these AI systems continue to evolve, the possibilities for creative expression will only expand, making this an exciting time to explore the intersection of language and visual art. Keep experimenting, maintain a curious mindset, and don't be afraid to try unconventional approaches. The most impressive AI images often come from prompts that break the rules in interesting ways. Happy prompting!

blocks.text: Writing an effective AI image prompt in 2026 is a different skill than it was two or three years ago. Models have become more capable of interpreting nuanced instructions, more consistent in their outputs, and more sensitive to the quality and specificity of the prompts they receive. This guide covers everything you need to know to write prompts that produce high-quality, repeatable results across the major AI image generators available today.
The Anatomy of a Strong Prompt

Every effective AI image prompt has a recognizable structure, even when it does not look like one. The structure consists of five layers: subject, context, style, technical parameters, and exclusions. You do not need to include all five layers in every prompt, but knowing them lets you diagnose why a prompt is not working and which layer needs adjustment.

The subject layer is the core element the image should depict. This is usually a noun phrase: a woman, a mountain, a glass of wine, a futuristic city. The subject should be specific enough to constrain the model without being so narrow that it has nothing to work with. A woman is too vague. A 30-year-old woman with short silver hair wearing a red coat gives the model useful constraints while leaving room for creative interpretation.

The context layer describes where the subject exists: location, environment, time of day, weather, season. Context is what separates a subject from a scene. A woman standing at a window becomes a specific moment with a woman standing at a rain-streaked apartment window at 3am, city lights blurred beyond the glass. The context does not need to be elaborate, but it should be present.

The style layer communicates the visual language of the image. This is where you specify photorealism versus illustration, cinematic versus editorial, high contrast versus muted tones. Style terms can reference artistic movements such as Art Deco or Impressionist, specific media such as oil painting or watercolor or 35mm film, or technical approaches such as long exposure or macro photography.

The technical parameters layer covers camera and output specifications: aspect ratio, focal length, aperture, depth of field, resolution quality descriptors. These terms work best with models trained on photography metadata and professional production documentation. They tell the model not just what to show but how to show it.

The exclusions layer is what many users skip. Negative prompts tell the model what to avoid. Common exclusions include: blurry, watermark, extra limbs, duplicate subjects, text overlay, overexposed, flat lighting. Always use this layer when you know the common failure modes for your subject type.
How Models Read Your Prompt

Understanding how an AI model processes your text helps you write better prompts. Most modern image generators use a text encoder that converts your prompt into a numerical representation, which the image generation model then uses to guide the denoising process. The text encoder has a limited token budget, typically 77 tokens for CLIP-based models, though newer architectures handle longer inputs.

Because of this token limit, word order and position matter. Elements that appear earlier in a prompt generally carry more weight than elements at the end. The model pays more attention to a cinematic portrait of a woman than to a woman, cinematic portrait. Put the most important creative decisions first and let supporting details follow.

Redundancy is a common mistake. Writing photorealistic, realistic, photograph, real, ultra-realistic uses up token budget repeating the same concept five times. One well-chosen term, such as photorealistic or 35mm photograph, is more effective than a stack of synonyms. The model does not add them together; it averages across them, often producing a muddied result.
Platform Differences in 2026

Each major platform has distinct strengths and prompt preferences. Gemini responds well to descriptive, natural-language prompts with detailed scene descriptions. It performs particularly well on portraits, architectural visualizations, and photorealistic natural environments. It is more sensitive to lighting and atmosphere descriptions than to camera specification terms.

Midjourney favours aesthetic keywords and style references. Artist name combinations and art movement references produce strong results. Its default output tends toward the dramatic and stylized, so prompts that want realism need to push back against this tendency with explicit photographic language.

DALL-E 3, accessed through ChatGPT, responds well to conversational prompt language and concept-level descriptions rather than technical specifications. It excels at following complex compositional instructions and unusual conceptual combinations.

Stable Diffusion and its variants give the most direct control through explicit negative prompts, LoRA model weights, and checkpoint selection. The base prompt language benefits from photography and illustration terminology, and the negative prompt field should be used extensively for quality control.
A Practical Iteration Workflow

The most effective approach to prompt writing is systematic iteration rather than prompt-by-prompt experimentation. Start with a simple version of your concept: three to five words that capture the core subject and style. Generate several variations. Evaluate what is working and what is not. Then add one specific improvement at a time and generate again.

Keep a prompt log. When you get a result that is close to what you want, record the exact prompt, the platform, and the settings. When you make changes that improve it, record those changes too. Over time you will build a personal library of prompt patterns that work reliably for the types of images you create most often.

Version your prompts. A prompt that works well today may produce different results after a model update. Save the specific model version or checkpoint alongside the prompt so you can reproduce the exact output if needed.
Common Mistakes to Avoid

Overloaded prompts are the most common mistake. When you ask an AI to produce a cinematic portrait with perfect lighting, fantasy elements, photorealistic textures, abstract background, and a complex emotional expression all at once, you are asking the model to optimize for conflicting objectives. The result is usually a compromise that satisfies none of them particularly well. Simplify.

Unspecified style assumptions are the second most common mistake. If you have a clear visual reference in mind but do not communicate it, the model has to guess. The more specific your style reference, the more likely the output matches your mental image.

Ignoring aspect ratio is a mistake that affects composition significantly. A portrait orientation prompt will be cropped differently than a widescreen orientation, and the composition that works in one format may not work in another. Always specify your intended output format before generating, not as an afterthought.
Building Your Personal Prompt Library

The most productive long-term approach to AI image generation is building a curated library of prompts that work reliably for your specific use cases. Start by categorizing your prompts by subject, style, and platform. Keep the best version of each prompt type and annotate it with notes about what works and what to watch out for.

Share prompts that work particularly well and collect prompts from other practitioners. The prompt engineering community generates and publishes high-quality prompt collections across dedicated libraries like AIPromptNest and forum communities. Testing other people's prompts against your own gives you insight into techniques you might not have discovered independently.

Revisit your prompt library regularly. As models improve and new platforms emerge, prompts that once required long detailed descriptions may become achievable with shorter, cleaner instructions. Periodically test your archived prompts against current models and update them to take advantage of improved capabilities.

blocks.text: Prompt engineering for AI image generation has evolved from a trial-and-error hobby into a structured discipline with repeatable techniques. The gap between a beginner who gets inconsistent results and an experienced practitioner who produces reliable, high-quality images on demand is largely a matter of understanding and applying a set of core principles. This guide covers the most effective prompt engineering techniques for AI image generation in practical terms.
The Specificity Principle

The single most important principle in prompt engineering is specificity. Vague prompts produce vague outputs. When you write a beautiful landscape, you are asking the model to decide what kind of landscape, what time of day, what weather, what colour palette, what camera perspective, and what mood. The model makes all those decisions for you, and they may not align with your vision.

Replace abstract quality words with concrete visual descriptions. Instead of beautiful, describe what makes the scene beautiful: golden hour light warming a mountain meadow, wildflowers catching the last light, long shadows stretching toward camera, mist in the valley below. This gives the model specific instructions it can execute, rather than a subjective judgment it has to interpret.

The same principle applies to style descriptors. Cinematic is more specific than cool-looking, and anamorphic widescreen with teal-and-orange grade is more specific than cinematic. Specificity at every level of the prompt reduces the model's need to guess and increases the chance that the output matches your intention.
Controlling Composition

Composition is one of the most underspecified aspects of most prompts. If you do not tell the model how to frame the shot, it will default to a visually balanced, centered composition that is technically correct but rarely interesting. Experienced prompt engineers use photography and cinematography terminology to direct the framing precisely.

Shot type vocabulary gives you the most direct control over framing: extreme close-up means face fills the frame, close-up means head and shoulders, medium close-up means chest and above, medium shot means waist and above, wide shot means full figure, extreme wide shot means figure is small in the environment. Each creates a different emotional relationship between the viewer and the subject.

Camera angle vocabulary controls the power dynamic and perspective: eye-level is neutral and objective, low angle makes the subject appear powerful and dominant, high angle makes the subject appear small and vulnerable, bird's eye view is top-down and map-like, Dutch angle creates tension and unease through diagonal tilt, and point of view gives a first person perspective.

Depth of field instructions control focus and visual hierarchy. Specifying shallow depth of field or wide aperture at f/1.8 tells the model to blur the background and foreground, isolating the subject. Deep focus or small aperture at f/16 keeps everything sharp from foreground to background. These terms work reliably with most modern image generators.
Lighting Techniques That Actually Work

Lighting descriptions have an outsized impact on the mood and quality of AI-generated images. The reason is that lighting is one of the most systematically documented aspects of photography and film, which means models have extensive training data linking lighting descriptions to specific visual outcomes.

Natural lighting terms provide reliable results: golden hour means warm low-angle sunlight shortly after sunrise or before sunset, blue hour means cool soft indirect light just before sunrise or after sunset, overcast diffuse means flat even shadowless daylight, and harsh midday means high-contrast short shadows and bleached colours. Each produces a recognizably distinct look that models reproduce consistently.

Studio lighting setups also translate well: Rembrandt lighting creates a dramatic triangle of light on the shadow side of the face, butterfly lighting places the key light directly above the face and is flattering for portraits, split lighting puts half the face in shadow and is dramatic and high-contrast, and rim lighting comes from behind the subject to separate them from the background.

Practical light sources add naturalism and narrative: candlelight, firelight, neon signs, monitor glow, street lamps, lanterns. When you specify that a subject is lit by the glow of a laptop screen, you are giving the model both a light quality which is cool, directional, and low intensity, and a narrative context that enriches the image.
Style Reference Techniques

Style references are among the most powerful tools in prompt engineering. The most direct form is referencing a known artist, photographer, or filmmaker whose visual style you want to evoke. Lighting in the style of Roger Deakins will produce something different from lighting in the style of Gordon Willis, and both will be meaningfully different from generic cinematic lighting.

Film and photography era references are particularly useful because they imply a complete set of technical and aesthetic characteristics. 1970s colour film grain and saturation implies a specific palette, a warm colour cast, visible grain, and characteristic light-leak behaviour. 1990s grunge editorial photography implies desaturated colours, high contrast, available light, and imperfect composition.

Art movement references work similarly. Baroque implies dramatic chiaroscuro lighting, rich deep colours, and theatrical grandeur. Impressionist implies visible brushwork, atmospheric colour rather than sharp edges, and a focus on light quality over precise form. Brutalist implies raw concrete, monumental scale, austere minimalism, and geometric composition.

When combining style references, be intentional. Baroque portrait with cyberpunk neon lighting is a viable creative direction where the contradiction is the point. Impressionist landscape with photorealistic detail is contradictory in a way that confuses models because the two references make incompatible demands on texture and edge quality.
Iteration Strategies for Better Results

Effective prompt engineering is an iterative process, not a one-shot activity. The most common mistake beginners make is to write a long, complex prompt in a single attempt and then be disappointed when the result does not match their mental image. The professional approach is to start simple, evaluate honestly, and add specificity where the output falls short.

When a generated image is close to what you want but not quite right, identify the one thing that most needs improvement. Is the lighting wrong? Is the composition off? Is the colour grade not matching your vision? Address only that element in the next iteration. Changing multiple elements at once makes it impossible to know which change produced the improvement.

Use seed values when a platform provides them. A seed number locks the random starting point of the generation process, so adding or removing a single term from the prompt shows you exactly what effect that term has in isolation. This is the most reliable way to understand how individual prompt elements influence the output.

Build variation from a working base rather than starting from scratch for each new image. Once you have a prompt that produces the composition and style you want, save it as a template. Swap subject descriptions, change locations, and adjust the mood while keeping the structural and style instructions intact.
Quality Control Checklist

Before submitting a prompt for generation, run through this checklist. Does the prompt have a clear, specific subject? Does it include a context or environment? Does it specify a lighting setup? Does it reference a visual style or aesthetic? Does it specify the output format or composition? Does it include exclusions for common failure modes relevant to the subject? If any of these are missing, adding them is likely to improve the result.

After generating, evaluate the output against these same criteria. If the subject is wrong, refine the subject description. If the lighting is flat, add lighting instructions. If the style is generic, add more specific style references. This systematic evaluation turns each generation into a learning opportunity rather than a coin flip.

The challenge is that anime style covers an enormous range of aesthetics, from the soft pastel-washed character designs of slice-of-life shows to the high-contrast detail-saturated art of shonen action series and the painterly cinematic compositions of Studio Ghibli films. This guide breaks down the best anime AI prompts by style category and explains the prompt mechanics that make each work.
Understanding Anime Visual Language

Before writing anime prompts, it helps to understand the visual conventions that define anime as an art style. The most recognizable feature is character design: large expressive eyes with detailed iris gradients, simplified nose and mouth, stylized hair that communicates personality and moves dynamically, and proportions that vary significantly by genre.

Backgrounds in anime are often painted in a more realistic style than the characters, creating a distinctive contrast between the stylized foreground figures and the detailed environment behind them. This is especially pronounced in Studio Ghibli productions, where backgrounds are painted with almost watercolour-like softness while characters are drawn in clean flat cel animation style.

Colour in anime is typically more saturated and less naturalistic than photographic colour. Skin tones range from pale white to warm tan, hair can be any colour including impossible ones such as blue, pink, silver, and green, and clothing often features bold contrasting colours that would look theatrical in real life but work within the anime aesthetic framework.

Lighting in anime frequently breaks physical rules for emotional effect. Characters can glow in darkness, dramatic lens flares appear without a light source, and shadow shapes are often simplified to single-colour flat areas rather than graduated tones. This stylized lighting is a feature, not a bug, and including it in your prompts produces more authentic anime-looking results.
Shonen Action Style Prompts

Shonen action anime has a distinctive high-energy visual style: bold lines, dynamic poses, dramatic power effects, and compositions that emphasize movement and force. These prompts work best when they specify the energy and scale of the action, not just the character design.

blocks.text: Prompt Tips Specific to Anime Style

Several prompt engineering techniques work specifically well for anime-style generation. First, model and style specifiers matter more for anime than for photorealistic content because anime encompasses such a wide aesthetic range. Terms like detailed anime style, cel shaded, clean lineart, soft painterly anime, and specific show or studio references all produce meaningfully different results.

Character design consistency requires detailed description of hair colour and style, eye colour and shape, clothing, and any distinctive features. Anime character designs are highly specific in ways that photographic subjects are not, and hair colour, eye size and detail, and outfit design are all core to a character's visual identity.

Background treatment in anime is distinct from character art. Specifying detailed painted background with simple character linework captures the characteristic Ghibli look. Flat colour background with detailed character produces a different more graphic novel aesthetic. Bokeh background with sharp character mimics the photographic anime art style popular in recent productions.

Emotion and expression are central to anime. Specifying not just the action but the emotional state, such as determined expression, embarrassed blush, surprised tears, or fierce battle focus, helps the model capture the expressive character of anime illustration rather than the more neutral facial expressions common in photorealistic outputs.

blocks.text: Photorealism is the most technically demanding category in AI image generation. A cinematic image can get away with dramatic stylization and an abstract image can be anything. But a photorealistic image is immediately compared against real photographs by everyone who sees it, and any deviation from physical reality registers as a flaw. This guide provides 100 photorealistic AI prompts organized by subject, along with the technical prompt strategies that make photorealism work.
What Makes Photorealism Work

Photorealistic AI image generation succeeds when the model has clear technical anchors that ground the image in photographic reality. The most important anchors are camera and lens specifications, natural or controlled lighting descriptions, skin and material texture language, and depth of field parameters. Without these anchors, the model's output tends toward a polished rendered look that reads as digital art rather than photograph.

Camera and lens terms provide strong photorealistic anchors because they reference the physical constraints of real photography. An 85mm portrait lens at f/1.8 with shallow depth of field tells the model to reproduce the specific compression, background separation, and focal plane characteristics of that lens at that aperture. Shot on a full-frame DSLR versus shot on a medium format camera produces subtly different rendering characteristics that experienced viewers recognize.

Lighting in photorealism must obey physical laws, or at least appear to do so. Light must have a source, cast shadows in the direction opposite the source, fall off with distance, and interact with surface materials in physically plausible ways. Specifying the lighting setup completely gives the model a detailed scenario to reproduce.

Skin texture in portrait photography is a major differentiator between photorealism and digital art. Real skin has pores, subtle subsurface scattering that makes skin glow slightly when backlit, fine hair and vellus fuzz, and non-uniform colour with slight variations in warmth and saturation across different areas of the face. Terms like skin texture detail, subsurface scattering, and natural skin imperfection help models produce more realistic skin rendering.

blocks.text: Strategy for Consistent Photorealism

The prompts above share several structural characteristics that make them produce reliably photorealistic outputs. First, they include a specific context or genre reference such as documentary portrait photography, commercial food photography, or architectural photography with tilt-shift, which tells the model what professional photographic tradition to draw from.

Second, they specify lighting in concrete terms: a named technique, a light source, a position, or a quality. Generic terms like good lighting or nice light produce inconsistent results. Specific terms like single softbox from above left or north-facing window light, overcast sky diffuser give the model a lighting setup it can reproduce.

Third, they mention a lens or focal length in contexts where it matters. The choice between a 24mm wide-angle lens and a 200mm telephoto produces dramatically different compression, perspective, and depth-of-field characteristics that are core to how a photograph reads.

Fourth, they avoid contradictory aesthetic instructions. A prompt that asks for photorealistic photography and artistic stylization in the same prompt creates a conflict the model has to resolve by blending them, producing a result that is neither fully photorealistic nor fully stylized. Choose one primary aesthetic direction and support it consistently throughout the prompt.
